mappings.note: Asks what is shared in series vs parallel (same I vs same V) across four bulb cases - the defining behaviour of the two combinations, so LO-2 rather than LO-1 alone; LO-1 is second because parts (c)/(d) need V=IR to see why unequal resistances give unequal PDs.

Ranks three drawn arrangements by equivalent resistance, so LO-2 not LO-3: the resistors are identical and only the topology changes. LO-5 added because the answer is unobtainable without reading the circuit figure.
Single unknown resistor, one battery: pure substitution into R=V/I. No combination and no geometry, so LO-2 and LO-3 are both wrong siblings.
Tests that resistivity is a material property independent of length, thickness and shape - exactly the length/area/material discrimination LO-3 names. Not LO-1: no V, I or R value is involved.

Fuse placement and melting on overcurrent - LO-2 is the only outcome that names the fuse. The series/parallel word in the assertion is about wiring a safety device, not about computing an equivalent resistance, so LO-2 of C 2.4 does not apply.

Needs Q=It then n=Q/e. No learning outcome in this set covers the definition of current as charge per unit time or the quantisation of charge; the competency text is the only row that names current as a circuit characteristic. Recorded as a content gap.

The whole task is recognising a correctly wired diagram (ammeter in series, voltmeter across the component) - the circuit-symbol half of LO-5. No numerical relation is graded, so no C 2.4 outcome is being probed.
Maximum resistance from five equal resistors means choosing series over parallel and summing - LO-2. Distinct from the plain-substitution Ohm's law items because no V or I appears at all.
Brightness is dissipated power, so C 2.5-LO-1 rather than any resistance outcome; LO-5 because the ranking depends entirely on where each bulb sits in the drawn circuit.

Graded output is heat in joules from H=I^2Rt, which only C 2.5-LO-2 covers; C 2.4-LO-2 is the genuinely separate first step (series sum to get the 1 A). Not C 2.5-LO-1: the answer is asked in joules over 5 s, not as power or kWh.
Two graded steps: I=P/V from the kettle rating (LO-1) and then the fuse rating chosen above it (LO-2). Pairing both is what separates this from the bare power-calculation family.

Only asks which quantity is common in series and which in parallel for two unequal resistors - a statement about the combinations themselves, with no equivalent value or Ohm's law substitution demanded.
The wattages are a distractor; the single graded fact is that series current is common. Deliberately not C 2.5-LO-1 - no power or energy is computed even though the items are rated bulbs.

Recall of the unit of electric power via P=VI. LO-1 is the only outcome that owns power and its units; kWh appears as a distractor option, which is energy, and the item turns on telling the two apart.

Match-the-column spanning the ohm defined as volt per ampere (LO-1) and resistivity measured in ohm-metre plus the superconductor row (LO-3). Both are needed because no single outcome covers the unit of R and the unit of rho.

Rows pair Ohm's law with V=IR and ohmic proportionality (LO-1) against resistivity varying with area (LO-3). The fourth row, current as charge/time, has no outcome in this set - see the gap noted on the electron-count item.

Table mixes resistance against length and against area (LO-3) with two small series/parallel networks whose equivalent value is asked (LO-2) and their currents from V/R (LO-1). All three are genuinely separate graded rows here, unlike the single-relation matching items above.
Same split as the other unit-matching item: ohm as 1 volt per 1 ampere (LO-1) versus resistivity depending on the matter of the conductor and the zero-resistance superconductor (LO-3).

Four drawn networks ranked by current drawn (equivalent resistance, LO-2) and by bulb brightness (power, C 2.5-LO-1), neither obtainable without reading the diagrams (LO-5). This is the one item in the part where all three axes are graded.

Choice of copper for connecting wires is a material-property judgement, the 'material' clause of LO-3. Not LO-1: no circuit quantity is calculated, and conductivity is the reciprocal of resistivity, not of resistance.
Doubling length doubles R via R = rho*l/A - the length clause of LO-3 stated as a proportionality rather than substituted numerically.

Compares 200 W and 100 W lamps through R=V^2/P, i.e. reasoning about the power rating of an appliance. Not C 2.5-LO-2: nothing about the heating mechanism of the filament is graded, only the wattage-resistance relation.

Heater wire requirements justified by H=I^2Rt and melting point - the heater clause of LO-2. Chosen over C 2.5-LO-1 because the reasoning is about heat produced and the wire surviving it, not about power consumed or billed.

Short circuit is named explicitly in the C 2.4 competency text but in none of its three outcomes, so the competency is the honest primary; LO-1 is second because the argument is V=IR with external R driven to zero. The internal-resistance/emf step is above the Class 10 outcomes entirely.
Pure meter-prediction item: what an ideal ammeter and an ideal voltmeter read in a given circuit, which is the second half of LO-5 verbatim. No C 2.4 outcome is graded because no value of R is used.
